summary: A snapshot of which protocols were official Internet standards, along with Best Current Practice documents, as of July 2001. It was a status listing rather than a complete index of the RFC series, and was one in a long line of such lists. It was replaced by RFC 3000. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A school posts a list showing which rules are official this year. This was that list for Internet protocols, and a newer list replaced it.

questions: list of official internet protocol standards
subtitle: The IETF's snapshot of standards and best practices as of summer 2001.

tldr.problem: The Internet has hundreds of specifications (RFCs) at different maturity levels. Engineers, operators, and policy makers also need guidance on best practices for operating the Internet, not just technical standards.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists every protocol the IETF considers an official Internet Standard, plus those in earlier stages of standardization (Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental) and Historic protocols. It also introduces Best Current Practice (BCP) documents, which offer operational guidance on topics like security, resource allocation, and IETF procedures.
tldr.outcome: This edition represents a shift in how the IETF organizes knowledge: it now includes both technical standards and operational best practices. Each category is listed by number, with both official numbers (STD for standards, BCP for best practices) and RFC numbers, capturing the landscape as of July 17, 2001.

today: RFC 2900 is Historic. The IETF no longer publishes periodic snapshots of this form; current standards information is maintained online at the RFC Editor website. The Best Current Practice track that RFC 2900 formalized remains an important part of the IETF standards process.

sections.title: What this document covers
sections.content:
RFC 2900 is a standards and best practices status document published by the IETF in August 2001. It describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as of July 17, 2001. This edition is notable for introducing a new category: Best Current Practice (BCP) documents, which are operational and procedural guidelines rather than technical protocols.

The document lists technical protocols by standardization level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic) and also organizes BCPs, which provide guidance on topics like Internet resource allocation, security recommendations, and IETF procedures themselves.
sections.eli5: This is the IETF's official list of Internet protocols and best practices from 2001. It's the first edition to officially include best practice guides alongside technical standards.

sections.title: Standards and best practices
sections.content:
Technical protocols move through the IETF standardization process: from Proposed Standard, to Draft Standard, to Internet Standard (the highest level). Experimental RFCs are for research, and Historic RFCs are obsolete or retired protocols.

Best Current Practice (BCP) documents are separate from this track. BCPs provide guidance on how to operate the Internet: address allocation policies, security recommendations, naming conventions, IETF procedures, and operational requirements for critical infrastructure like DNS root servers. They carry the weight of community consensus without being technical specifications.
sections.eli5: Protocols are the rules for how computers talk. Best practices are the rules for how people should operate and manage the Internet. This document lists both kinds.

sections.title: The lists
sections.content:
The document is organized into sections by type: Standard Protocols (listed both by STD number and by RFC number), Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols, Best Current Practices (listed both by BCP number and by RFC number), Experimental Protocols, and Historic Protocols. Each entry shows the title, protocol name (if assigned), and numbers.

Asterisks mark entries that changed status since the previous edition. This makes it easy to see what moved from one maturity level to another, what new BCPs were created, and what protocols were retired.
sections.eli5: Each category (official standards, trials, old rules, best practices) is organized by number. Stars show what changed since the last edition.

sections.title: The living standards and practices list
sections.content:
This RFC documents a snapshot in time, but the IETF maintains an updated list daily on the RFC Editor web site. The snapshot approach is useful for historical reference, showing exactly what was official on a given date.

RFC 2900 added the formal Best Current Practice track, reflecting the reality that the IETF produces operational guidance as well as technical specifications. This structure has persisted: the standards process continues to publish both standards (STD) and best practices (BCP) alongside one another.
sections.eli5: This list shows what the Internet community agreed was both technically and operationally correct in summer 2001. The IETF keeps a live updated list, but this snapshot captures that moment in time.
